entries.topicDescription: Powerful enumerations with associated values and pattern matching.

tips.title: Enums with associated values model state precisely
tips.content:
Swift enums can carry associated values — each case stores
different data. This lets you model states precisely,
eliminating impossible combinations.

Instead of a class with optional fields (where you have to
wonder "which fields are valid in which state?"), each enum
case declares exactly the data it needs.

This is perfect for network results, loading states, and
navigation routes. The compiler forces you to handle every
case, preventing missed states.

Associated values can be any type: tuples, structs, other
enums, or even closures. Each case is independent.

tips.title: Pattern matching with switch and if-case
tips.content:
Swift's switch statement is exhaustive — you must handle every
case of an enum. This catches bugs at compile time when you
add a new case.

Use 'let' bindings inside case patterns to extract associated
values. You can also add 'where' clauses for conditional
matching within a case.

For single-case checks, 'if case' and 'guard case' avoid a
full switch statement. These are handy when you only care
about one specific case.

Pattern matching also works with tuples, ranges, optionals,
and even custom types that implement the ~= operator.

tips.title: Recursive enums with indirect cases
tips.content:
Sometimes an enum case needs to hold another instance of the
same enum — for example, modeling a tree or an arithmetic
expression. This creates a recursive type.

Swift requires you to mark recursive cases with 'indirect'.
This tells the compiler to store that case as a reference
(pointer) instead of inline, avoiding infinite size.

You can mark individual cases as indirect, or the entire
enum. Recursive enums combined with pattern matching let
you build and evaluate tree structures elegantly.

This pattern is common in parsers, expression evaluators,
and any domain with naturally recursive data structures.
